extracted.intended_audience: DHS adjudicators, immigration attorneys, stakeholders, and members of the public interested in public charge rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and factors for determining whether a noncitizen is "likely at any time to become a public charge" for admissions or adjustment of status under the INA, as articulated in DHS's final rule and its responses to public comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not all public benefits considered
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS has determined that not all public benefits should be considered in public charge inadmissibility determinations because not all benefits are equally indicative of primary dependence on the government for subsistence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS excludes certain supplemental or special-purpose benefits from consideration because they are less probative of primary dependence and their inclusion would add little value for officers while deterring eligible noncitizens and family members from seeking benefits; examples and further discussion appear elsewhere in the rule (e.g., SNAP described as supplemental and work-supporting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on primary dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: Public charge determinations should focus on primary dependence on the government for subsistence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS interprets this focus by reference to public cash assistance for income maintenance and long-term institutionalization at government expense in particular, while acknowledging that courts and past guidance also considered the immigrant's ability to prospectively support themselves (age, profession, family, assets, employability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular indicia: public cash assistance and long-term institutionalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Receipt of public cash assistance for income maintenance or institutionalization for long-term care at government expense are key indicators of being "primarily dependent" on the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows the 1999 Interim Field Guidance which defined public charge by either (i) receipt of public cash assistance for income maintenance or (ii) institutionalization for long-term care; DHS considers these categories especially probative when evaluating primary dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider amount, duration, and recency of benefit receipt
rubrics_metrics.description: When considering past, current, and future receipt of public benefits, DHS takes into account the amount, duration, and recency of receipt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These temporal and quantitative dimensions help determine how probative benefit receipt is of primary dependence; they are considered alongside other factors in the totality of the circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality of the circumstances analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The determination of whether an alien is likely to become a public charge is a prediction based upon the totality of the alien's circumstances at the time of application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No single factor is outcome-determinative; the fact that an alien has been on welfare does not, by itself, establish likelihood of becoming a public charge. DHS will weigh statutory and other factors together to reach a predictive judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: IIRIRA-specified minimum factors
rubrics_metrics.description: By statute (IIRIRA), officials must consider at a minimum: age; health; family status; assets, resources, and financial status; and education and skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These mandated factors form the baseline of analysis; DHS and officers may also consider an Affidavit of Support under section 213A. The rule treats these as required components of the assessment, considered within the totality of circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of education and skills and related evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS is considering a noncitizen's education and skills, as evidenced by degrees, certifications, licenses, skills obtained through work experience or educational programs, and educational certificates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education and skills serve as indicators of future employability and self-support; DHS may also consider work history and other record information when assessing likelihood of public dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noncitizen may be inadmissible without complete or permanent dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS's inquiry may determine that a person is inadmissible on public charge grounds even when the record suggests a level of dependence that is less than complete or permanent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule allows DHS to find likelihood of becoming a public charge based on a combination of factors that indicate substantial risk of dependence, not only on evidence of total or permanent dependency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of non-governmental sources of support
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of friends, relatives, or other private sources willing and able to provide assistance is relevant and can weigh against a finding of likely becoming a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Past decisions (e.g., Matter of Martinez-Lopez) support that private support availability reduces the likelihood of future public dependence; officers should consider offers or indications of private assistance in the totality analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Past receipt of benefits is not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of past or current receipt of public benefits alone does not automatically establish that an individual is likely to become a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precedent and DHS's position emphasize that prediction requires looking beyond mere receipt to other circumstances (e.g., employability, family support, assets). The Board of Immigration Appeals has held past welfare receipt 'does not, by itself' establish likelihood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit of Support (Section 213A) consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: An enforceable Affidavit of Support under section 213A of the INA may be considered in public charge determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress identified the affidavit as a potential factor; DHS may weigh the existence and strength of such a sponsor's support in assessing likely public dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: DHS's discretionary authority to define and apply public charge
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress provided discretion by using language such as 'in the opinion of,' and the INA authorizes the Secretary of Homeland Security to promulgate rules to guide public charge determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS asserts broad interpretive authority to define 'likely at any time to become a public charge' and to decide which public benefits are considered; this discretion underlies the regulatory choices in the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: No fixed numerical threshold of benefit receipt
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress rejected defining 'public charge' to include any alien who receives means-tested benefits for an aggregate of at least 12 months; courts and DHS have not fixed a quantifiable standard of level or duration that alone determines public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS and the courts have generally declined to quantify the level or type of public support required for an inadmissibility finding, reinforcing reliance on qualitative, contextual factors rather than bright-line numeric rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local labor market conditions not a regulatory factor
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS has not designated local labor market conditions as a regulatory factor to determine whether a noncitizen is likely at any time to become a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While courts (e.g., Gegiow) discussed labor market conditions historically, DHS's rule focuses on individual economic and support-related factors rather than local employment market conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude weight on non-cash benefits (except institutionalization) per prior guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Earlier guidance (1999 Interim Field Guidance) stated officers should not place any weight on the receipt of non-cash public benefits (other than institutionalization) for public charge determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS notes this historical approach and aligns parts of the rule with the idea that non-cash benefits are generally less probative of primary dependence; the final rule explains differences from prior rules and which benefits are excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule aims for clarity, fairness, and consistent adjudication
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule is intended to be a faithful execution of the public charge ground that is clear and comprehensible and that would lead to fair and consistent adjudication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS states the rule is promulgated to implement the public charge ground in a manner that avoids unequal treatment and undue barriers, and DHS intends to issue additional guidance for officers and the public to clarify application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of medical/mental incapacity and inability to earn a livelihood
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors such as mental or physical disability, incapability of earning a livelihood, or being certified for senility are relevant to assessing likelihood of becoming a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (e.g., Wallis, Harutunian) indicates that evidence of incapacity and lack of private support that would render a person unable to self-support for a reasonable length of time weighs toward a public charge finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity to chilling effects on benefit uptake
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS recognizes that expanding the list of benefits considered could deter eligible noncitizens and family members (including U.S. citizens) from seeking important supports, and this potential chilling effect is relevant to policy decisions about which benefits to consider.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS weighed the likelihood of deterrence of public benefit use (e.g., medical care, preventive services, SNAP for children) in deciding to exclude certain supplemental or special-purpose benefits from public charge consideration.
